en: The Ritual Manual for Vajraśekhara Yoga Homa,
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master of Daxingshan Monastery, the Śramaṇa Da Guangzhi Bukong,
who was promoted to the rank of Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial by Imperial Decree.
I shall now explain the homa; by means of this, swift accomplishment is attained.
Through the ritual procedures of the homa practice, one remains in correspondence without interruption.
All such matters should be performed according to the vidyā-mantra.
Performing homa according to the respective categories, one achieves the unsurpassed activity.
Homa is said to be of many kinds; briefly stated, there are five types.
The extensive explanation is found in the Great Yoga, as taught in the Secret Doctrine.
I shall now briefly explain the play of the Vidyādhara through the ritual of homa,
by which the maṇḍala of the family is accomplished.
There are five types of homa, each of which has many varieties.
Pacification and enrichment, the third is subjugation,
summoning as the fourth, and the fifth is magnetizing;
of these five types of homa, magnetizing is the most excellent.
I shall now explain the ritual of Kuṇḍa according to the yoga of correspondence:
for pacifying, the hearth should be perfectly circular;
it should be made square for increasing prosperity; and triangular for subjugation.
The Vajra-form Mañjuśrī is supreme for summoning;
the long lotus-form corresponds to the rite of attraction.
Having thus explained these five types, Mañjuśrī’s activities are unsurpassed.
The rite for pacifying should be performed during the first watch of the night; the rite for increasing should be performed during the first part of the day;
the rite for subjugating should be performed during the middle part of the day according to the fierce methods;
the rite for summoning may be performed at any time; and the rite for magnetizing should be performed during the final watch of the night.
These five yogas constitute the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) for performing ritual actions:
one should face north to perform rites of pacification (*śāntika*); face east for rites of increase (*pauṣṭika*);
and face south when performing rites of subjugation (*abhicāruka*).
Gazing upward toward all directions is the ritual for summoning;
if performing the rite of magnetizing, one should face west.
For pacifying, one binds the Buddha-mudrā; for increasing prosperity, the insignia of the Jewel.
Vajra Wrath brings subjugation; Vajra Hook performs summoning.
When the great summoning is in resonance, the Lotus Family brings loving-kindness.
Thus, through these five yogas, one should perform the homa rites.
For the rite of pacification, burn sweet wood; for increase, use fruit-bearing wood;
for subjugation, use bitter wood; for summoning, use thorny wood;
for magnetizing, use flowering wood—these are the five kinds of wood.
The practitioner should employ them as follows:
for the rite of pacification, a wheel; for increase, a three-pronged vajra; for subjugation, a single-pronged vajra;
for summoning, one should use a hook; and for magnetizing, a lotus.
The hearth for pacifying (śānti) should be measured with a full cubit in width and half a cubit in height;
for increasing (puṣṭi), it should measure two cubits [in width] and half a cubit in depth.
For subjugating (abhicāra), it should have the form of Kumbhaka, being triangular with each side measuring one cubit.
For the hook-summoning [mandala], it is one cubit in length, with both width and depth reduced by half;
for the rite of attraction (*vaśya*), it is also one cubit, with width and depth like those of the hook-summoning.
The five types of Mañjuśrī mandalas should be drawn as threefold layers.
In the central court, draw a ritual vajra, with lotus flowers at the four corners;
in the second court are the four mudrās, namely the four pāramitās,
as offerings within the four corners.
The celestial retinues of the eight directions, the four corners at the four gates, and the four outer offerings of the means of attraction;
in the center is established the Honored One Samantaprabha.
This is the *śāntika* (pacifying) Mañjuśrī, while the other four possess the characteristics of Mañjuśrī.
The three enclosures are all thus.
In the central enclosure, one should increase the representation by painting the Ratnakarma;
in the second enclosure, one should paint the retinue of Ratnasambhava Buddha.
The third enclosure and its gates are also as previously described.
In the central court, there is a single-pronged *karmavajra* for subjugation; lotuses should be drawn in the four corners.
In the second enclosure, one should paint the retinue of Trailokyavijaya.
The four wrathful aspects;
the third courtyard and its gates are also as previously described, all possessing wrathful characteristics.
To summon [the deities] into the central courtyard, one should draw a vajra hook.
In the four corners, draw lotus flowers;
in the second enclosure, one should paint the retinue of Akṣobhya;
in the third enclosure, at the four corners, the eight directions, and the four gates, it is as described for the first Krodha, Kuṇḍalin.
In the central court, one should reverently depict the Lotus Karma [deity] with a three-pronged vajra at each of the four corners;
in the second court, one should depict the retinue of Amitāyus and the four venerable ones.
In the four corners of the third court, as well as the eight directions and the four gates, it is explained just as before.
These are the five homas taught in the Yoga Tantra; the practitioner should know them.

The rim of the hearth is two finger-widths high and four finger-widths wide; the base of the hearth’s opening within the rim is two finger-widths wide. Inside this, the ritual seal (mudrā) is two finger-widths high. The portion of the hearth near the body has an upright neck that is four finger-widths wide and two finger-widths long; next, it widens to ten finger-widths and is four finger-widths long. Beyond that, it is fashioned in the shape of a lotus so that the proportions are harmonious; from the top of the upright neck to the tip of the petals, the total measure is twelve finger-widths. Both the height and depth are level with the rim. These five types of hearths are all identical in these respects.
The method for purifying the ground is according to the Great Maṇḍala rite.

One performs the mudrās for digging the earth and holding the spade, etc., by forming the vajra-bond with the thumbs, middle fingers, and ring fingers extended, and recites the mantra twenty-one times.

The mantra is: Oṃ nikhaṇavastuti svāhā. To consecrate the clay, cow dung, and unguents, perform the following mudrā: join the palms of both hands; bend the second joints of the index fingers (tarjanī) and the little fingers (kaniṣṭhā) so they touch; extend the middle fingers (madhyamā) and ring fingers (anāmikā) together; and hold the thumbs (aṅguṣṭha) and forefingers (tarjanī) upright, with the tips of the forefingers forming the shape of a mouth. Recite the mantra twenty-one times.
The mantra is:
Oṃ āḥ mṛtu navava hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. The empowerment of the five-colored powders and the mudrās, as well as the mantra, are all as described in the *Yogatantra*.

Consecrate the ghee, honey, curd, milk, as well as wood, the five kinds of grain, incense, flowers, and so forth, each with seven recitations of the Vajrakarma Bodhisattva mantra. For the mudrā, join both hands such that the *jñāna* (middle) and *sūci* (ring) fingers pinch the *śīla* (forefinger) and *tarjanī* (index finger) nails; then extend the remaining three fingers upward like the shape of a vajra, crossing them so that the right hand presses down upon the left.

The mantra is: *Oṃ vajrakarma jaḥ*. All the *homa* fuel sticks to be burned should be placed on the right side; the clarified butter (*ghṛta*) should be placed upon a lotus-leaf stand; honey, curd, milk, and rice gruel should be placed near the right side of the hearth; two vessels of fragrant water should be set on the left side. These vessels may be made of gold, silver, refined copper, white porcelain, or conch shell—all are equally suitable. The fragrances include white sandalwood, turmeric, camphor, and so forth. One vessel is used for sprinkling the fire and the offering materials, while the other is used for the holy assembly and the fire deities to rinse their mouths.
For the *śodhana-mudrā* (sprinkling purification seal): with the thumb and ring finger joined (*dhyāna-bandha*), extend the index fingers (*tarjanī*) and open them three times. The mantra is:

*Oṃ āḥ mṛte hūṃ phaṭ*. For the *mukha-śodhana-mudrā* (mouth-rinsing seal): form a vajra-fist with the right hand, extend the middle finger (*tarjanī*), stir the water seven times while reciting the mantra for empowerment, then cup the water with the right hand and, lowering the hand toward the body, sprinkle it to the right as an offering to the fire.
The mantra is: Oṃ Vajranāthavajra-dam.

For the pacifying rite (śāntika), the principal deity, the fire god, the hearth, the robes, the food, and the flowers are all white. One assumes the auspicious posture (bhadrapīṭha), with both legs crossed and upright, the right knee pressing upon the left, in correspondence with a mind of loving-kindness (maitrī).
For all rites of augmentation, use yellow and sit in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*).
For all rites of subjugation, use black and sit in the squatting posture (*utkuṭukāsana*), treading with the big toe of the left foot upon the big toe of the right foot.
For summoning (*ākarṣaṇa*), all [implements] are red, and [the deity] sits in the half-lotus posture (*ardhaparyaṅka*).
For the rite of loving-kindness (*vaśīkaraṇa*), the color is the same as for summoning; [the deity] sits in the *bhadra* posture, with one leg extended and the other foot hanging down.

For the invitation (*āvāhana*), from the *samaya* mudrā up to the invitation itself, one follows the original ritual manual (*mūlavidhi*), or follows whichever of the five types of *homa* is appropriate, according to the fivefold manifestation of the body (*pañcākārābhisambodhi*) of the respective family lord (*kulādhipati*).

Having invited [the deities], recite praises and establish the noble assembly through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*). Surrounded by the hearth-altar (*kuṇḍa-maṇḍala*), one then offers *argha* water. Each person binds their respective *karmamudrā* to take their place, displays their respective *samaya*, and recites the *homa-mantra* one hundred and eight times. Thereafter, taking a flower, empower it three or seven times with the *Agnideva-mantra* and cast it into the fire. Then, bind the *Agnideva-mudrā*: grasp the right wrist with the left hand, extend the palm of the right hand outward, bend the *dhyānāṅguṣṭha* (thumb) across the palm, and move the *pradeśinī* (forefinger) back and forth like a hook.
Having performed the invitation and the offering, one proceeds from the *dhyāna-pāramitā* to the *prajñā-pāramitā*, whereby the dismissal is accomplished.
The mantra is as follows: Oṃ e hi e hi ma hā bhu ta.
mṛdvāriścinivajrasattvamahānirghātamo-hara-maśāntisandhupāvaḥ.
Ahoṇaye haviye kaviye nāha nāyā svāhā.
Having welcomed [the deity], sprinkle them three times with scented water and rinse their mouths three times; then, using the root mantra,
ladle out three full ladles of clarified butter with a large spoon and cast them into the fire, visualizing them entering the mouth of the Fire God and reaching his heart-lotus.

The mantra is: *Oṃ āgneye svāhā*. This same mantra is also used for the consecration (*adhiṣṭhāna*). With this mantra, one should cast the ladle three times into the honey, curd, milk, wood, and even the incense and flowers. One should visualize the Fire Deity with four arms: the right hand in the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya-mudrā*), the second hand holding a rosary, the left hand holding a staff (*khaṭvāṅga*), and the second [left] hand holding a water jar (*kuṇḍikā*). One should imagine that from the heart, throughout the body, there flow forth immeasurable clouds of unguents, clouds of flowers, clouds of burning incense, and various offerings of food, drink, and lamps, making offerings to all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, Śrāvakas, and all worldly deities.
At the end of the *homa* mantra, "svāhā," recite the name of the object of one's request and cast it [into the fire].

Thereafter, perform an offering of three full ladles with a large ladle; empower a single flower and place it at the seat in its original direction, then invite [the deity] out of the furnace and return to the original seat. Next, purify the fire three times, and with the four-syllable vidyā, invite the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, each to sit upon their respective seats.

For the third offering, rinse the mouth; then, fill three large ladles to the brim and present them as offerings. Thereafter, with the small ladle, offer three libations each of honey, curdled milk, milk porridge, and rice mixed with curd, followed by wood, the five grains, incense, and flowers, each presented three times. Visualize that these enter the mouth of the Honored One, while maintaining a sincere mind.
In the rite for pacifying calamities (*śāntika*), one must add ten times as much oil to the five grains; for the wood, use one hundred and eight, fifty-four, or twenty-one pieces.
The mantra is:

*Oṃ sarvabodhanāhavanavajraye svāhā*. According to some teachings, one may employ the Family Mother (*kuleśvarī*) for pacification, or the mantra of the principal deity (*iṣṭadevatā*), or the mantra of Vairocana; in all cases, by placing "svāhā" at the beginning, one prays for the removal of all calamities for oneself and others.

Focus the mind on the noble assembly within the hearth; imagine that from the pores of the entire body, outside the heart, clouds and oceans of offerings flow forth, reaching infinite worlds to make offerings to all Buddhas and to eliminate the suffering and afflictions of all three evil realms.

Having performed the homa, offer three full ladles to the noble assembly; then, gather the remaining grains, incense, flowers, and so forth into a single vessel and offer them to the worldly deities of the ten directions.

If performing a rite of augmentation (*puṣṭi*), first invite the Fire Deity as previously described, and immediately offer the three large ladles to the assembly of noble ones, along with agarwood, flowers, and the like, while burning non-glutinous rice.

If one wishes to perform a rite of prolonging life (*āyuṣya*), burn *kūṭaja* grass; the hearth for prolonging life is as before for the rite of augmentation, but with the shape of armor drawn outside the hearth. The non-glutinous rice and *kūṭaja* grass should be ten times more than other materials.
The mantra for increasing [merit] is:
*Oṃ vajrapuṣṭaye svāhā*. The mantra for prolonging life is: *Oṃ vajrayuṣe svāhā*.
To the "svāhā" at the end, add the words of whatever wish is in one's heart.

Focus the mind on the noble assembly within the hearth. Visualize that from the pores of the bodies of the noble assembly, clouds and oceans of offerings flow forth from their hearts to reach infinite worlds, making offerings to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. Furthermore, these offerings illuminate and touch all sentient beings across the six realms and four modes of birth, causing them all to attain prosperity, wealth, honor, and long life.

Then, by means of this very light, one should visualize the rain of the seven treasures and all necessary articles falling within one's own home; furthermore, one should visualize the celestial nectar pouring down into oneself, permeating every pore.

If performing a rite of subjugation (*abhicāra*), first invite the Fire Deity as previously described. Using radish, mustard oil, buffalo ghee, or *rūdraka* seeds, first offer three large ladles to the assembly of noble ones. Then, using scentless flowers, foul-smelling flowers, *guggulu* incense, salt, poisons, and so forth—or using only iron filings—fashion an effigy (*mānuṣa*) of the person to be targeted, and cut it into pieces, casting them into the fire.

At the time of casting the fire offering, visualize that from the heart of the Fire Deity, weapons flow out from within his body and are cast upon the person; visualize both the Fire Deity and the Principal Deity as being in wrathful form.
The mantra is:
HŪṂ VAJRASATTVA YE PHAṬ. Add the name of the person concerned above the word "PHAṬ."

Alternatively, using the mantra of this very rite, or that of Acala, Trailokyavijaya, Mañjuśrī, or the Six-Limbed Honored One (Ṣaḍbhuja), one should visualize clouds and oceans of weapons and implements flowing forth from the bodies of the wrathful deities to make offerings to all the wrathful deities throughout the entirety of space; these very weapons shall then descend upon that person's house and body.

If performing the rite of summoning (ākarṣaṇa), it is done exactly as for the rite of augmentation (puṣṭi), with the sole exception that the flowers used must be red flowers from a thorny tree, or else the substances prescribed for burning in the root ritual.
The mantra is:
HŪṂ VAJRAKARṢAYA JAḤ. Add the name of the person to be summoned after "JAḤ."

One should then visualize that from outside the heart of the Honored One, immeasurable vajra hooks flow forth from his entire body to make offerings to all Buddhas and noble ones throughout the reaches of space. With these many hooks, one summons sentient beings of the three evil realms and establishes them in the virtuous states of humans and devas; then, with these same hooks, one enters their hearts and draws them forth.
If performing the rite of subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*), it is identical to the above, with the sole exception that one uses red flowers, or the substances prescribed in the specific ritual manual.
The mantra is:
*HŪṂ VAJRĀVEŚAYA JAḤ*. Add the name of the person to be targeted before *JAḤ*.

One should then visualize flower-arrows flowing forth from the body of the Honored One, pervading immeasurable worlds to make offerings to all Buddhas and noble sages; they also strike the hearts of those seeking detachment among the pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas, as well as the hearts of mutual hatred and anger among the beings of the six realms and four modes of birth. With these many arrows, one then strikes that person in five locations: namely, the forehead, the two breasts, the heart, and the lower part, which refers to the private organ.
Next, the method for *samāpatti* is explained: place the object to be accomplished before the vessel of clarified butter; if the object is large, place it to the left or right side, as convenient.

The practitioner’s body, the vessel of clarified butter (*ghṛta*), the substance to be offered, the fire-pit, and the assembly of deities—these five collections should be established in their proper sequence around the perimeter. Taking a small ladle and filling it with clarified butter, one adds it to the substance being offered while reciting the mantra up to the syllable *svāhā*. Immediately upon reaching *svāhā*, one lifts the ladle and casts it into the fire; it descends simultaneously with the sound of *ha*. One then prolongs the sound of *ha* so that the ladle returns to the substance, and only when the sound of *ha* finally ceases does the offering conclude.
Just as one empowers a person, place it upon the tip of the ladle.
If the mantra of the chosen deity does not contain the syllable "svāhā," you should add it and recite it.
If one performs empowerment from a distance, one may either write down the person's name or place it upon their clothing, then focus the mind and perform the empowerment.
If there is no clarified butter (*ghṛta*), using milk instead is also permissible.

Having made the offerings, one presents three full ladles of oblation to the assembly of noble ones using a large ladle, followed by three sprinklings and three rinsings. Taking a small ladle, one recites the mantra for extinguishing evil destinies (*pāpadeśanā-mantra*) and performs seven or twenty-one *homa* offerings for the sake of all sentient beings, then mentally escorts the noble assembly back to their original seats.

Using the four-syllable vidyā, invite the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) of the ten directions into the fire-pit. Perform the ritual rinsing and cleansing as before, and immediately cast the remaining incense, flowers, ghee, honey, and so forth into the fire. Recite the respective root mantras once or three times for each deity, appending the specific object of one's request to the word *svāhā*. Then, form the *karmamudrā* and *samayamudrā* of the assembly of holy ones, recite praises and make aspirational prayers. Form the Trailokyavijaya mudrā, rotate it counter-clockwise to dissolve the boundary, and finally perform the ritual of dismissal according to the rules for recitation.

Then, having exited the maṇḍala, one should spread *kuśa* grass, lotus leaves, or other green grass at the eight corners of the maṇṍala; or, having smeared a circular altar, one should establish ten positions. To the left and right of Śakra in the eastern direction, one places Brahmā and Mahendra. If there is no space within the maṇḍala for these positions, one should separately demarcate a square boundary in front of the maṇḍala, create eight directions therein, and establish two positions in its center for Brahmā and Mahendra.

In the east is Śakra, riding a white elephant and dwelling amidst five-colored clouds; his body is golden in color, his right hand holds a trident at his heart, his left hand supports his left hip, and his left foot hangs down.
The three goddesses each hold a lotus; they carry blue lotuses on platters, or various flowers and the like upon platters.

The mantra is: *Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ indrajāya svāhā*. To the southeast is the Fire Deity (*Agni*), riding a blue sheep, with a flesh-colored body and flames emanating from his entire form. His two right hands hold a green bamboo staff and a water jar (*kamaṇḍalu*); his two left hands have one palm raised and the other holds a rosary.
Two celestial maidens holding heavenly flowers stand to the left and right of the ascetic seer;
they drape their left legs over and their right feet under [the seer's shoulders].
The mantra is as follows:

*Namo samantabuddhānām oṃ āne svāhā*. To the south is Yama-deva, riding a water buffalo; his right hand holds a banner topped with a human head, and his left hand is held with the palm facing upward. He is attended by two goddesses, and two yakṣa messengers hold swords and halberds. He is dark red in color and stands with his right foot extended.

The mantra is: *Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ jvālaya svāhā*. To the southwest is the Lord of the Rākṣasas, riding a white lion and clad in armor. His right hand holds a sword held upright; his left hand has the thumb pressing down upon the middle and ring fingers. He is red-fleshed and white.
Two celestial maidens attend him on his left and right, and two rākṣasa demons hold three-pronged tridents.
The mantra is:

*Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ nārtyai svāhā*. To the west is Varuṇa, Lord of Waters; he dwells within the water riding upon a tortoise, is light green in color, holds a sword in his right hand and a dragon-noose in his left, and has five dragons upon his crown.
The four celestial maidens hold exquisite flowers.
The mantra is:

*Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ varuṇāya svāhā*. In the northwest is the Wind Deity (*Vāyu*), riding upon a deer amidst the clouds and clad in armor. His left hand supports his hip, and his right hand holds a single-pronged spear with a red banner atop it.
Two goddesses attend him, along with a host of yakṣas.
The mantra is:

*Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ vāyave svāhā*. To the north is Vaiśravaṇa, seated upon two spirits, wearing armor on his upper body; his left palm supports a stūpa, and his right hand holds a jeweled mace; his body is golden in color.
The two goddesses hold precious flowers and other offerings.

The mantra is: *Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ veśravaṇāya svāhā*. To the northeast is the deity Īśāna—formerly called Mahesvara or Maheśvara, also known as Maheśvara—who rides a yellow, fat ox. His left hand holds a skull-bowl filled with blood, and his right hand holds a three-pronged trident. He has a pale, flesh-colored complexion, three eyes, and a wrathful expression; two fangs protrude upward, and he wears a necklace of skulls. Within his crown are two crescent moons facing upward.
The two goddesses holding flowers have the mantra:
*Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ īśanāya svāhā*. The mantra of Brahmā from the zenith is as follows:

*Namo samantabuddhānām mṛḍaṅginī svāhā.* In the center, one should visualize the four-armed Acala, with a complexion like raw meat. His two hands each form a vajra-fist; the index and little fingers of each hand are bent into the shape of hooks, which he places at the corners of his mouth as if they were fangs. His right hand holds a sword held upright, and his left hand holds a noose. He sits upon a flat rock in the half-lotus posture (ardhaparyaṅka), with the right leg pressing down upon the left. His majestic flames and radiant light pervade his entire body like fire.
The mantra for the Earth Deity of the lower direction is: *Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ pṛthivīye svāhā*.

For the offerings to the deities of the ten directions, prepare a mixed porridge consisting of *śāli* rice, sesame seeds, and mung beans cooked together. Place this in a single vessel. At each seat, set out a clean leaf. First, take a pure water flask filled with scented water and pour a small amount onto the leaf as an offering. Next, offer scented unguent by flicking it with the fingers. This is followed by flowers, incense, and music.

Take one ladle of gruel and empower it three times with the respective root mantra. Then, using a small wax candle or a paper candle, insert it into the gruel. Focus your mind on offering this; do not allow the flame to go out until the [recitation] is complete. Append the words of your specific aspiration to the end of "Svāhā."
The mantra of the Seven Luminaries is:
*Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ nairātmya-śvārī-prapada-tiryati-ra-maya svāhā*. The mantra of the Twenty-eight Lunar Mansions is:

*Namo samantabuddhānāṃ namo narakṣaśiṣṇurute svāhā.* Within the eight directions, two positions correspond to the zenith and nadir; the offerings for all are identical, yet it may also be used individually if there is a specific aspiration.
If within the homa altar, one establishes the mind by marking each according to its direction.
I shall now explain the characteristics of the pouring ladle (sruc) and the writing ladle (sruva);
by performing the accomplishment (*sādhana*) with these, the reciter will swiftly attain success.
The ladle should be one cubit in length; it should be made of khadira wood, firm and dense, without holes or cavities.
Its mouth should be exquisitely well-formed, four finger-widths in width, and its depth should be one finger-width.
It should be made as beautiful and majestic as the form of Śrīputra; it should be coarse enough to hold a handful,
and one cubit in length like a ladle.
The wood should be as previously described, or *khadira* wood;
its depth should be half that [of the width]. Within it, one should fashion a lotus, and likewise employ a vajra.
Thus the Great Sage has taught: one who seeks *siddhi* should perform the *homa*, and success will be swiftly achieved.
The *Vajraśekhara-yoga-homa-vidhi* (金剛頂瑜伽護摩儀軌) states in the *Baja Mipilu* (八家祕錄):
"One fascicle of the *Vajraśekhara-yoga-homa-vidhi*, translated by Amoghavajra; recorded in the *Zhenyuan xinding shijiao mulu* (貞元新定釋教目錄) by Hai-ren Yun-zhen."

*Homa-vidhi*, one fascicle. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master from Siṃhala, the Śramaṇa Amoghavajra; his name was changed to Zhizang by imperial decree. It is slightly more extensive than the previous version.
"Since the translation by Zhizang is already included in the Ming Canon, it contains corruptions and omissions, such as the absence of the images of the eight devas;
this [version] is not like that.
Furthermore, there are differences in the detail or brevity of the text, so it is appropriate to preserve both versions."

Therefore, based on the edition collated by Master Yōzan Myōzui at Tōji Temple during the sixth *bính-tử* year of the Bảo Lịch era, and further compared with the copy from the Kōwa 5th year held in the Sōikei-bō scriptural repository, this was carved for longevity. Recorded in the fifth month of the *hìn-tị* year, the first year of the Hiung Hòa era, by the śramaṇa Kuaidào, a resident of Fǔyān.
